title: Formless, beyond compare
hook: arupe hain, anupe hain: without form, beyond comparison (Jaap, chachari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, kripaal, the Merciful, right after the Timeless, and your line, salute mercy. Today the rhythm changes again, and the lines get very short.

Better than yesterday. Worse than her. Not as tall, as fast, as rich, as liked. The mind is a measuring machine. It can hardly look at anything without setting it beside something else and checking which is bigger. A sunset gets compared to last week's. A child gets compared to a cousin. A few minutes of scrolling, and the comparisons pile up. Then a hymn says, in two words, that there is something nothing can be set beside.
screen: `BETTER THAN, WORSE THAN, NOT AS.` → `THE MIND IS A MEASURING MACHINE.` → `SOMETHING NOTHING CAN BE SET BESIDE.`

segments.voice: Further on, Jaap moves into a meter called chachari, and its lines are startlingly short: two words each. Aroop hain. Anoop hain. Ajoo hain. Abhoo hain. After the snake's long glide, it feels like quick footsteps, or a heartbeat. Hain means You are, so each line is a tiny sentence. Today, the first two, which the glide already saluted as aroope and anoope. Aroop: roop is form, shape, appearance, and the small a means without. You are formless. Nobody can paint You, sculpt You, put You on a screen. Sikhs take this seriously: there are no statues of God in a gurdwara, and the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, sits where you might expect an image. Then anoop, from upma, comparison, likeness: the One with nothing to compare to. The two words lean on each other. Comparison needs shapes. To say this is bigger than that, you need a this and a that, each with an outline. With no form, there's nothing to measure against. Beyond compare isn't a boast that God wins every contest. There's no contest at all. So every morning, before the comparing starts, a Sikh reciting Jaap spends a few seconds saluting the one thing that can't be ranked: a small rest for the mind, where better than and worse than simply don't apply.
screen: `CHACHARI: TWO WORDS A LINE.` · `AROOP: WITHOUT FORM.` · `ANOOP: NOTHING TO COMPARE TO.` · `NO SHAPE, SO NO CONTEST.` · then, large: `BEYOND COMPARE.`

segments.voice: Look at one thing in front of you, a cup, a plant, your own hand, the sky in the window, and let it be just this. Each time the mind says nicer than, older than, not as good as, smile at it and come back: not better, not worse, here. If you pray, you can say aroop hain, anoop hain softly.
Formless. Aroop hain, anoop hain: You are without form, and beyond compare, in the short, quick lines of Jaap's chachari meter.
Your line: beyond compare. With no shape, there's nothing to measure the One against. Day three hundred thirty-nine, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the short chachari lines of Jaap Sahib briskly each morning, and gurdwaras keep no images of God: the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of words, is the center.

original.note: Gurmukhi: aroop, without form, from roop, form or appearance.

trapdoor: what you thought: formless means God is vague or invisible.
what it means: the One has no shape to picture and so nothing to be measured against.
what a scholar hears: anoop derives from upama, likeness; the chachari chhand packs each attribute into a two-word line ending in hain.

chat.says: Jaap calls the One aroop and anoop. Why would formless mean beyond compare?
options: Comparing needs shapes to set side by side; with no form, there's nothing to measure against.
Because the One always wins: whatever you set beside it, it comes out bigger.
Because comparing anything is forbidden in Sikh teaching, so nothing may be ranked.
chat.meaning: Aroop, formless, and anoop, beyond compare, lean on each other: with no outline, there's nothing to set beside the One, so no contest.
